study.title: JWST evidence for a sharp "Cosmic Daybreak" at z = 15

cover.headline: **Early JWST data may suggest galaxies ignited suddenly** at a specific moment, not gradually as expected

slides.title: The team reports that stellar ages in high-redshift galaxies converge to zero by z=15, with no earlier star formation.
slides.body:
JWST has found bright young galaxies out to z=14.5. But deeper searches for fainter, earlier ones now turn up only misidentified objects.

The stars in these distant galaxies all appear to have formed recently, with no older populations.

slides.title: The paper argues this sharp cutoff confirms a prediction of Wave Dark Matter models.
slides.body:
Standard dark matter predicts a gradual Cosmic Dawn. Galaxies should appear progressively fainter as you look back.

Instead, this early paper suggests a late, abrupt transition. That matches ultra-light boson dark matter, not heavy particles.

slides.title: In Wave Dark Matter, quantum pressure resists collapse until gas clouds reach 4 billion solar masses at z=15.
slides.body:
The team calculates a boson mass of 2.2 × 10⁻²² eV. That figure is similar to independent estimates from lensing and dwarf galaxies.

The highest-redshift galaxy luminosities converge to the predicted scale, not the lower values standard models expect.

caveats: This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has checked the work yet.
The interpretation depends on stellar age estimates, which carry large uncertainties at these extreme distances.
Wave Dark Matter remains a minority hypothesis. Most cosmologists work with cold dark matter made of heavy particles.

source.abstract: Luminous young galaxies have been uncovered with relative ease by JWST, extending to z=14.5, so it is puzzling that deeper spectroscopy of fainter candidates now finds only interlopers. This redshift `ìmpasse" is underscored by the measured stellar ages of these high-z galaxies, which we show converge to zero by z=15, with a marked absence of earlier star-formation. Taken literally, such a late transition from the Dark Ages to luminous galaxies is unlike the gradual Cosmic Dawn of standard LCDM, but does confirm a key prediction of Wave Dark Matter, $ψ$DM, as a Bose-Einstein condensate. The de Broglie wave pressure resists gravity until a substantial Jeans mass of $4\times 10^9M_\odot$ is overcome at z$=$15, corresponding to a light boson $m_ψ=2.2_{-0.3}^{+0.4} \times 10^{-22}$eV, and similar to independent estimates from lensing anomalies and dwarf galaxies. Furthermore, the substantial luminosities of the highest redshift galaxies appear to converge to the initial Jeans scale of $ψ$DM, whereas LCDM predictions extend to lower luminosities and larger ages than observed. These contrasting predictions can be definitively tested as JWST observations accumulate, with diametric implications for Dark Matter as heavy particles beyond the Standard Model, or ultra-light bosons motivated by the String Axiverse.
